sections.content: Wholesaling real estate is one of the few investing strategies where you can generate serious income without owning a single property. No mortgage. No repairs. No tenants. Instead, you find deeply discounted properties, lock them up under contract, and sell that contract to a cash buyer for a profit. Assignment fees typically range from $5,000 to $20,000 per deal, and some wholesalers close multiple deals every month. If you're just getting started, bookmark the [Wholesale Real Estate for Beginners: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesale-real-estate-beginners-guide) — it covers the full landscape. This article breaks down the process into clear, actionable steps you can start today.
What Is Wholesale Real Estate (and Why It Works)

The core idea is simple: you act as the middleman between a motivated seller and a ready buyer. The seller wants out fast — maybe they inherited a property, are behind on payments, or just can't afford repairs. The buyer, usually a house flipper or landlord, wants a good deal without doing the legwork. You solve both problems and collect a fee for connecting the dots. No money is required to buy the house, just enough earnest money to secure the contract (often $500 to $1,000). That's what makes wholesaling one of the most accessible entry points in all of [real estate investing](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners).
Wholesaling is not about owning real estate — it's about controlling it long enough to profit. Your most valuable asset is your ability to find deals others can't see.
Step 1: Learn the Legal Basics in Your State

Before you send a single mailer or knock on a single door, understand the rules in your state. Wholesaling is legal in all 50 states, but a few have added restrictions around marketing unlicensed real estate. Some states require you to disclose your intent to assign the contract. Others have specific language requirements. Don't skip this step — it protects you from fines and deal blow-ups. Check out our [Is Wholesale Real Estate Legal? State-by-State Guide 2026](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/is-wholesale-real-estate-legal-state-guide) to see exactly what applies where you plan to operate.
Step 2: Choose Your Target Market

You don't need to wholesale in your backyard. Many successful wholesalers operate virtually in high-volume markets with strong investor demand. Look for cities with high population growth, a large renter base, and active flipping communities. Markets like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Houston, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/houston-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) consistently rank among the best for wholesale volume because they have motivated sellers and deep cash buyer pools. Pick one market, learn it inside and out, and master it before expanding.
Pro Tip: Pick a market with at least 50 active cash buyer transactions per month on public record. That tells you investors are already buying — you just need to bring them better deals.
Step 3: Find Motivated Sellers

This is where most beginners spend the most time, and rightfully so — your deal flow is everything. A motivated seller is someone who needs to sell quickly and is willing to accept below market value in exchange for speed and convenience. The most common lead sources include:

items: Direct mail: Send postcards to pre-foreclosures, vacant properties, or absentee owners. A 1% response rate on 500 mailers can produce 5 leads.
Driving for dollars: Physically drive neighborhoods looking for distressed properties — overgrown lawns, boarded windows, deferred maintenance.
Cold calling: Pull lists of tax-delinquent or probate properties and call owners directly.
Pay-per-click ads: Run simple Google or Facebook ads targeting motivated seller keywords in your market.
Bandit signs: Place 'We Buy Houses' signs at busy intersections. Old school, but still effective in many markets.
Networking: Connect with attorneys handling probate and divorce cases — they often know owners who need to sell fast.

sections.content: Step 4: Analyze the Deal and Make an Offer

Once you have a lead, you need to know your numbers before you ever open your mouth about price. The golden formula in wholesaling is: Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO) = After Repair Value (ARV) × 70% − Repair Costs − Your Assignment Fee. If a house would be worth $250,000 fully renovated, and needs $40,000 in repairs, and you want a $10,000 assignment fee, your offer ceiling is $125,000. Offer below that to leave room for negotiation. Use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run these numbers in seconds without doing the math by hand.
How to Estimate Repairs Accurately

You don't need to be a contractor, but you need a rough system. Walk the property with a simple checklist: roof age, HVAC condition, foundation cracks, kitchen and bath finishes, flooring, windows, and plumbing. A light cosmetic rehab might run $15–25 per square foot. A full gut renovation can hit $60–80 per square foot. When in doubt, estimate high — it protects your buyer's margin and your reputation.
Step 5: Get the Property Under Contract

When the seller agrees to your price, you sign a purchase and sale agreement that includes an assignability clause. This clause is non-negotiable — it gives you the legal right to transfer your position in the contract to another buyer. Your earnest money deposit (typically $500 to $1,000) goes into escrow and holds the deal while you find your end buyer. Set a realistic closing timeline: 15–30 days gives you enough time to market the deal without losing the seller's trust. Have a real estate attorney in your market review your contract template at least once to make sure it's airtight.
Step 6: Build and Market to Your Cash Buyer List

Your buyers list is your business. A great deal with no buyers is just a ticking clock. Start building your list before you even have a deal under contract. Pull cash transaction records from your county's public property records — anyone who bought without a mortgage in the last 12 months is a potential buyer. Attend local real estate investment association (REIA) meetings. Post in Facebook groups. The more buyers you have competing for your deal, the higher your assignment fee climbs. For a deeper dive on this, read [How to Find Cash Buyers for Wholesale Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/how-to-find-cash-buyers-wholesale) — it covers 11 proven sourcing strategies with scripts included.
Step 7: Assign the Contract and Collect Your Fee

Once a buyer is ready, you sign an assignment of contract agreement. This document transfers your right to purchase the property to the buyer in exchange for your assignment fee. The fee is typically collected at closing through the title company — you don't touch the purchase funds at all. The title company handles everything: verifying title, coordinating with the seller, and disbursing your check. Walk through this step with a wholesale-friendly title company at least once before your first deal so you know exactly what to expect.
What If the Deal Falls Through?

It happens. Buyers back out, inspections reveal surprises, sellers get cold feet. Always have a backup buyer on your list. If a deal falls through completely, review what went wrong — was your ARV off? Was the repair estimate too low? Did you rush the seller? Each failed deal is a learning opportunity. Read [7 Wholesale Real Estate Mistakes Beginners Make](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-real-estate-mistakes) to avoid the most common pitfalls before they cost you real money.
Building a Sustainable Wholesaling Business

One deal is exciting. Consistent deal flow is a business. Reinvest your first few assignment fees into better lead generation — more mailers, a CRM to track your leads, or a skip tracing service to find owner contact information faster. Track your metrics obsessively: cost per lead, cost per deal, average assignment fee, and days from contract to close. Wholesalers who treat this like a business from day one scale quickly. Those who treat it like a side hustle usually stay stuck. For a full framework on scaling, check out the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide.

Pro Tip: Your first deal will take the longest. Most new wholesalers close their first deal within 60–90 days of consistent action. After that, the systems kick in and deals start compressing to 30 days or less.
